name: Sitemap Examples
title: Sitemap Website Example: 8 Valid XML Samples to Copy
description: Copy-ready sitemap examples: urlset, sitemap index, image, video, news and hreflang sitemaps, each annotated — plus a 1-click check of any site's real sitemap.
answer: A sitemap is an XML file that lists the URLs you want search engines to find. The simplest sitemap website example is a urlset with one url and loc per page. Below are eight copy-ready samples — basic, index, blog, e-commerce images, video, news, multilingual and plain text — plus a live lookup of any real site's sitemap.
trust: Every sample follows the sitemaps.org 0.9 protocol and Google's extension namespaces; the live lookup fetches and validates a real site's sitemap.
body:
## XML Sitemap Example: urlset, Index, Image, Video and News

Every XML sitemap is one of two shapes. A **urlset** lists pages; a **sitemapindex** lists other sitemaps. The image, video, news and hreflang variants are a urlset with an extra namespace for the additional tags.

| Example | Root element | Extra namespace | Use it when |
|---|---|---|---|
| Basic / blog | urlset | none | Any site |
| Sitemap index | sitemapindex | none | Over 50,000 URLs or 50 MB |
| E-commerce | urlset | image | You want product photos found |
| Video | urlset | video | Pages built around a video |
| News | urlset | news | Publishers in Google News |
| Multilingual | urlset | xhtml | Same page in several languages |

The format itself is defined at [sitemaps.org](https://www.sitemaps.org/protocol.html).

## Which tags does Google actually use?

Only `loc` and, when it's honest, `lastmod`. Google says it [ignores priority and changefreq](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/sitemaps/build-sitemap), and uses lastmod only if it is consistently and verifiably accurate. That's why our samples leave priority and changefreq out entirely.

Two limits apply to every sitemap: 50,000 URLs or 50 MB uncompressed per file. Past either, split into several files and list them in a sitemap index.

## When do I need the special sitemaps?

Rarely, for most sites. Image tags help when product photos are loaded in ways Google can't discover on its own ([image sitemaps](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/sitemaps/image-sitemaps)). News sitemaps are only for publishers, and only for articles from the last two days, with at most 1,000 news entries per file ([news sitemaps](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/sitemaps/news-sitemap)).

If none of that applies, the basic example is all you need.

## How do real sites organize theirs?

Mostly with an index. When we checked 391 well-known sites in October 2026 ([dataset](/resources/ai-crawler-access-study-2026-10.json)), 84.6% pointed to their sitemap from robots.txt — the simplest way to make sure every crawler finds it. Use the live lookup above on a site you admire to see its structure.

## How do I check my own sitemap?

Paste your domain into the [sitemap checker](/tools/sitemap-checker): it finds the file through robots.txt, validates the XML and samples the URLs for errors. No sitemap yet? The [sitemap generator](/tools/xml-sitemap-generator) crawls your site and builds one.

faqs.q: What is the simplest valid sitemap?
faqs.a: An XML file with a urlset root element in the sitemaps.org namespace and one url entry containing a loc for each page. lastmod is optional but useful when it reflects real edits.

faqs.q: Where should I put my sitemap?
faqs.a: Usually at the site root, such as /sitemap.xml, and referenced from robots.txt with a "Sitemap:" line. You can also submit it in Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools.

faqs.q: Should I include priority and changefreq?
faqs.a: You can, but Google ignores both. Spend the effort on accurate lastmod dates instead, which Google uses when they consistently match real changes to the page.
